2. The 3-Minute Demo Script (Two-Column Table)

Practice this table with a stopwatch until you can deliver it smoothly in 2.5 to 3 minutes:

What I Do on Screen What I Say Aloud (Natural Fresher Voice)
Step 0: Starting Screen
Show http://localhost:3000 with the Dashboard already loaded and 3 sample monitors visible. 		"Hi! This is ChangeWatch, an intelligent website change detection platform I built to eliminate the pain of manually refreshing pages for exam alerts or price drops."
Step 1: Dashboard Overview
Point mouse to the top 4 stats cards: Total Monitors, Active Jobs, Healthy, and Changed. 		"Right here on the Dashboard, you see an immediate real-time overview: total monitored pages, active background worker jobs, and health states. Below, each card represents a monitored website with its check interval and noise filter settings."
Step 2: Add New Monitor
Click the green "+ Add Monitor" button in top right. A modal dialog opens.
Type:
• Name: Tech Headline Tracker
• URL: http://localhost:4000/demo/headline
• Check: Timestamps & Tokens filters ON.
Click "Save Monitor". 		"Let me add a new website to track. I paste the target URL, select an interval, and keep dynamic noise filters turned ON. When I click save, the Express backend validates the URL for SSRF security, commits it to SQLite, and immediately queues a baseline snapshot."
Step 3: Trigger Instant Check
On the newly added card, click "Check Now".
A blue pulse shows the worker fetching the page. Status turns to OK with a timestamp. 		"I can click 'Check Now' to trigger an immediate check. In the background, our worker launches headless Playwright, visits the site, captures the clean text, and stores Version 1."
Step 4: The Change Detection & Diff
Click on an existing monitor that says "CHANGED" (e.g. Demo: Headline).
Click the "View Diff" button. The app switches to the Compare page. 		"Now here is the core power of ChangeWatch: the Compare page. Notice how it computes an exact Myers word-by-word diff—green text highlights what was added, and red shows what was removed, exactly like GitHub commits. Above it, we have an interactive visual screenshot slider comparing before and after."
Step 5: Noise Suppression Magic
Switch to the Test Rig tab in the navigation bar.
Show the /demo/clock and /demo/counter test fixtures. 		"What makes web scraping notoriously unreliable is false alarms—live clocks and ads change every second. Notice our Test Rig: for pages with ticking clocks, our noise normalization engine replaces changing times with static tokens, so ChangeWatch stays green and never bugs the user unnecessarily."
Step 6: Responsive View Check
Right click -> Inspect -> Toggle Device Toolbar (Mobile View, e.g. iPhone 14). 		"The interface is built with Tailwind CSS, so the layout is completely mobile-responsive: navigation collapses neatly, and dashboard cards stack cleanly into a single column."
Step 7: Closing Line
Switch back to Desktop view on Dashboard. 		"In summary, ChangeWatch provides full-stack automated web monitoring with smart noise filtering, shared-fetch deduplication, and multi-channel alerting. Thank you! I'd love to answer any questions or dive into the code."

3. The "Wow Moment": What to Show for Maximum Impact

🌟 The Primary "Wow Moment": The Myers Diff & Visual Slider in Compare.tsx

Why it impresses: Most student projects simply say "website changed: yes/no". Showing a side-by-side color-coded git-style text diff with an interactive image comparison slider proves you built actual analytical algorithms, not just a toy wrapper.

How to pitch the Wow Moment:
"Look at this diff view: it's not just a binary alert. We implemented the Myers diffing algorithm on the server to pinpoint exact word additions and deletions, and paired it with Pixelmatch visual diffing for screenshots. This gives users 100% transparency into what changed."

5. Features to SKIP or AVOID in the Live Demo

⚠️ Do Not Test These in the Live Room:
  • AVOID Live Public Websites (Amazon, Flipkart, Google): Public e-commerce portals have aggressive bot-detection, CAPTCHAs, and dynamic JS that can take 15 seconds to load or block your IP on campus Wi-Fi. Always use the built-in local demo fixture URLs (http://localhost:4000/demo/...)!
  • AVOID Sending Real Test Emails: Unless you have an active SMTP server configured in .env, clicking "Send Test Email" will time out or throw a connection error. Stick to showing the UI config.
  • AVOID Gemini AI API Key live calls: If the venue Wi-Fi has high latency or your key runs out of quota, the AI summary might take 10 seconds. Show the rule-based summary instead.
  • AVOID Running npm run seed while demo is live: Re-seeding while the server is running might lock the SQLite database file for a split second. Seed before entering the room!

6. "Show the Code" Plan: 3 Files to Open

If an interviewer asks, "Can you open your editor and show me the code?", calmly open these 3 files:

File to Open Key Lines to Highlight What to Say Aloud
1. src/client/pages/Dashboard.tsx
(Frontend Component)		 Lines 25–45: useEffect fetching data from /api/dashboard/stats.
Lines 80–120: Card mapping & status badge rendering.		 "Here is my main React Dashboard. I use a clean hook-based architecture: useEffect queries our Express API on mount, stores monitors in state, and renders responsive cards with status-dependent Tailwind styles."
2. src/server/engine/changeDetector.ts
(Core Engine)		 Lines 30–60: Cheerio text extraction.
Lines 80–110: Myers diff calculation using diffWords.		 "This is the heart of ChangeWatch. We pass raw HTML into Cheerio, strip scripts and styles, apply our noise normalization filters, and run the Myers diff algorithm to compare the new text with the previous version in SQLite."
3. src/server/capture/routeValidation.ts
(Security)		 Lines 20–45: DNS resolution & ipaddr.parse() check. "Security is critical for web scrapers. Here we prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): before Playwright touches any URL, we resolve DNS and reject any private, loopback, or cloud metadata IP addresses."

7. Troubleshooting: What If Something Breaks in the Room?

Failure Scenario Quick Fix (Technical) What to Say Calmly to Interviewers
Server won't start:
Port 3000 already in use		 Kill existing node process in terminal:
npx kill-port 3000
or in PowerShell:
Stop-Process -Name node -Force
then re-run npm start.		 "Looks like my previous background process is still bound to port 3000. Let me quickly terminate it and restart the server."
Database locked error:
SQLITE_BUSY		 Delete changewatch.db-wal and run:
npm run seed		 "The database had an unclosed write handle from testing. I'm resetting the local SQLite database now."
Blank page in browser Hard refresh: Ctrl + Shift + R
Open DevTools Console (F12) to check for failed fetch.		 "Let me do a hard browser refresh to clear the cached bundle."
Campus Wi-Fi is completely down ChangeWatch works 100% offline! Use local fixtures: http://localhost:4000/demo/... "One great design feature of ChangeWatch is that it has a built-in local demo server with 16 fixtures, so it runs completely offline without campus internet."

9. Questions Interviewers Will Ask DURING the Demo

Q1: "Where does this data come from? Is it live or mock?"
"When running locally with npm start, this data is 100% live! It reads from our local SQLite database. On our static GitHub Pages deployment, it uses a mock adapter to showcase the UI without needing an active Node backend."
Q2: "What happens if I type an invalid URL like 'notawebsite'?"
"Our Express backend uses Zod schema validation. If the string is not a valid URL starting with http or https, it immediately rejects the request with HTTP 400 Bad Request and displays a friendly error banner in the React UI."
Q3: "How does your site prevent cross-site scripting (XSS) in the diff viewer?"
"React automatically escapes HTML entities inside JSX text nodes. We never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML for raw webpage content, ensuring any malicious JavaScript tags in the target site are rendered safely as plain text."
